To operationalise this standard, we recommend a risk-stratified approach to validation.

Our framework therefore requires version-specific validation, mandatory notification when healthcare-deployed models are updated, and defined revalidation triggers when model architectures change substantially.

We recommend mandatory incident reporting systems for translation-related adverse events, periodic comprehension audits using standardised protocols, patient feedback mechanisms to flag translation problems directly and defined trigger metrics that would prompt revalidation when error rates exceed specified thresholds.

Validation processes should therefore incorporate community health workers and cultural mediators from target language communities, not only bilingual evaluators.
This pathway applies to novel combinations, digitally under-represented languages (such as Haitian Creole, Tagalog or Hmong) or specific high-risk use cases lacking robust published evidence.
All validation studies should be prospectively registered in a public database analogous to ClinicalTrials.gov to prevent selective publication of favourable results.
These studies should use validated assessment protocols and be sized to detect clinically meaningful differences in patient understanding.

unlisted_practices: Establish federal oversight bodies within HHS or FDA with statutory authority to mandate pre-deployment validation of AI translation tools, conduct ongoing monitoring, and impose penalties for non-compliance.
Include translation experts, clinicians serving LEP populations, patient advocates from affected language communities, and health equity researchers on AI oversight bodies.
Create centralized validation consortia and federal funding mechanisms for validating AI translation for digitally under-represented languages.
Adopt a Universal Patient Comprehension Standard requiring AI translation to be non-inferior to certified human translation on patient comprehension.
Evaluate AI translation quality by patient comprehension and functional health literacy rather than linguistic accuracy alone.
Permit institutions to rely on robust published validation evidence for well-studied tool-language combinations while focusing on ongoing monitoring.
Require qualified human translator review of AI translations of critical documents before they are given to patients.
Establish liability standards that incentivize AI developers to conduct robust validation.
Govern transmission of protected health information to commercial LLM services to prevent unauthorized data retention or use for model training.
Disclose A/B testing in which users may unknowingly receive different model versions.
Foundation model providers should disclose granular performance metrics for medical use cases across languages.
